title: React Native skill test
summary: A timed practice assessment: multiple-choice questions on components, layout, lists, navigation, architecture, data, performance, releases and accessibility, plus two short coding tasks.

questions.prompt: What happens when this renders?
choices: It shows "Hello" in the default font
It throws: text strings must be rendered within a Text component
It renders nothing and logs a warning
questions.explain: In React Native only Text can render strings. A bare string inside a View is an error, unlike a div on the web.

questions.prompt: What does a View become on a device?
choices: A real native view on each platform
Nothing, until it has a Text child
An HTML div inside a hidden web view
A bitmap drawn by the JavaScript engine
questions.explain: React Native maps its components to native platform views. There is no HTML or DOM.

questions.prompt: Which component suits a short settings screen with a dozen fixed rows that must scroll?
choices: A View with overflow set to scroll
questions.explain: A ScrollView renders all its children at once, which is fine for a short, fixed set. Virtualised lists pay off for long or unbounded data. A View does not scroll.

questions.prompt: With no style, how are a View's children laid out?
choices: In a row, left to right
In a column, top to bottom
Stacked on top of each other
questions.explain: flexDirection defaults to column in React Native, unlike the web where it defaults to row.

questions.prompt: The parent fills the screen. What share of the height does the second child take?
questions.code:
<View style={{ flex: 1 }}>
  <View style={{ flex: 1 }} />
  <View style={{ flex: 2 }} />
</View>
questions.explain: flex values split the free space by ratio: 1 + 2 = 3 parts, so the second child gets two of them.

questions.prompt: What colour is the background when active is true?
questions.code:
const s = StyleSheet.create({ a: { backgroundColor: 'blue' }, b: { backgroundColor: 'red' } })
<View style={[s.a, active && s.b]} />
choices: red, because later styles override earlier ones
It throws, because style must be an object
blue, because the first style wins
questions.explain: Style arrays merge left to right, so later entries win. A false entry is skipped, so this pattern makes conditional styles easy.

questions.prompt: Why is FlatList better than items.map inside a ScrollView for 5,000 rows?
choices: ScrollView cannot scroll more than 1,000 rows
FlatList renders rows on a background thread
FlatList sorts the data for you
FlatList only renders rows near the viewport and drops the rest
questions.explain: FlatList virtualises: it keeps a window of rows around the viewport mounted. A ScrollView mounts every child, which costs time and memory.

questions.prompt: Rows hold local state such as an expanded flag. Rows can be deleted. Which key is safest?
choices: The item's stable id from the data
No key: FlatList works it out
questions.explain: A stable id lets React match each row to the same component after inserts and deletes. Index keys move state to the wrong row, and random keys remount every row.

questions.prompt: Every row is exactly 72 points tall. What does adding getItemLayout give you?
choices: FlatList can skip measuring and jump straight to any index
questions.explain: With known heights, FlatList can compute offsets itself, so scrollToIndex works for rows not yet rendered and layout work drops.

questions.prompt: Screen A pushes screen B on a stack. The user goes back. What happens?
choices: B is popped and unmounted; A was mounted the whole time and keeps its state
Both screens unmount and the stack resets
B stays mounted but is hidden
A remounts and loses its state
questions.explain: A stack keeps lower screens mounted. Going back pops and unmounts the top screen and reveals the one beneath with its state intact.

questions.prompt: What is the best thing to pass as a param when opening an order details screen?
choices: A ref to the previous screen
The whole order object with its methods
The order id, then load the order on the details screen
questions.explain: Params should be small and serialisable so deep links and saved navigation state work. Pass an id and load the data where it is shown.

questions.prompt: A screen must refresh its data every time the user returns to it. Why is useEffect with [] not enough?
choices: It is enough; it reruns on every focus
useEffect does not run in React Native
The screen stays mounted under the stack, so a mount effect runs only once
questions.explain: Screens below the top of a stack stay mounted, so mount effects do not rerun on return. Use the navigator's focus event or focus effect hook.

questions.prompt: On Android, what is padding?
questions.code: const padding = Platform.select({ ios: 20, android: 12, default: 0 })
questions.explain: Platform.select returns the value for the current platform, and falls back to default only when there is no matching key.

questions.prompt: A folder has Picker.ios.tsx and Picker.android.tsx. How should other files import it?
choices: Use require with a Platform.OS check
It cannot be imported; both files must be merged
questions.explain: The bundler resolves ./Picker to the platform-specific file when it builds for each platform.

questions.prompt: In an Android back button handler, what does returning true mean?
choices: Let the default back action run
You handled the press, so the default back action is skipped
questions.explain: Returning true consumes the event. Return false to let the navigator or system handle it.

questions.prompt: What does JSI change compared with the old bridge?
choices: JavaScript now runs on the UI thread only
JavaScript can hold references to native objects and call them directly, without serialising JSON messages
Apps no longer need a JavaScript engine
questions.explain: The old bridge batched asynchronous JSON messages. JSI lets JavaScript call into C++ host objects directly, and even synchronously when needed.

questions.prompt: Why does Hermes improve start-up time?
choices: It skips rendering the first screen
It compiles JavaScript to bytecode at build time, so less work happens on launch
It runs JavaScript on the GPU
It removes unused native modules at runtime
questions.explain: Hermes ships precompiled bytecode, so the device does not parse and compile the bundle on each launch.

questions.prompt: What is a key benefit of TurboModules?
choices: They load lazily, the first time JavaScript uses them
They let modules run without native code
They render views faster than Fabric
questions.explain: Old native modules were all set up at start-up. TurboModules load on first use, which helps start-up time, and are called through JSI.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this hook?
choices: Effects cannot subscribe to native events
The listener is never removed, so it leaks and keeps firing after unmount
questions.explain: Return a cleanup from the effect that calls subscription.remove(), so each mount adds one listener and unmount removes it.

questions.prompt: Which need most clearly calls for writing a native module?
choices: Formatting dates in the user's locale
Calling a platform SDK that has no JavaScript API
questions.explain: Native modules bridge to platform features that JavaScript cannot reach. Pure logic belongs in JavaScript.

questions.prompt: In the new architecture, what does codegen use as input?
choices: A typed spec file that describes the module's interface
questions.explain: You write a typed spec, and codegen generates the native interface so JavaScript and native code agree on types at build time.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this reducer?
choices: It mutates state, so React may not see a change and skip the re-render
It must return undefined for unknown actions
questions.explain: Reducers must be pure and return a new object. Return { ...state, items: [...state.items, action.item] } instead.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between server state and client state?
choices: There is no difference in practice
Server state is a copy of data owned elsewhere, so it can go stale and needs caching and refetching
questions.explain: Data from an API is a cached snapshot. It needs loading and error states, refetching and invalidation, which is why it is often handled by a data-fetching cache.

questions.prompt: An optimistic "like" fails on the server. What should the app do?
choices: Roll back to the previous state and tell the user
Retry forever without telling the user
questions.explain: Optimistic updates show the change before the server confirms. On failure, restore the saved previous state and show an error.

questions.prompt: Where should a refresh token be stored?
choices: The platform secure store, such as Keychain or Keystore
A file in the app bundle
questions.explain: Async key-value storage is not encrypted. The secure store encrypts at rest and is the right place for credentials.

questions.prompt: Async key-value storage only stores strings. How do you save a settings object?
choices: JSON.stringify on write and JSON.parse on read
Store each key in a separate app
Pass the object; it is converted for you
questions.explain: Serialise with JSON.stringify, and parse on read inside a try so corrupt data does not crash the app.

questions.prompt: A new release changes the shape of stored data. What is the safest approach?
choices: Clear all storage on every launch
Assume the old data matches the new shape
Store a schema version and migrate old data when the app starts
questions.explain: Users upgrade from any older version. A stored version number lets you run migrations step by step.

questions.prompt: A request hangs on a poor connection. What does fetch do by default?
choices: Waits with no timeout of its own
questions.explain: fetch has no built-in timeout. Use an AbortController and a timer to abort slow requests.

questions.prompt: A queued "create order" request is retried after a timeout. How do you avoid creating two orders?
choices: Send an idempotency key so the server can spot the repeat
questions.explain: The first request may have succeeded even though the response was lost. An idempotency key lets the server return the original result instead of acting twice.

questions.prompt: The network listener says the device is connected. What can you safely assume?
choices: Only that there is a network connection; requests can still fail
questions.explain: Being connected does not mean the internet or your server is reachable. Always handle request failures.

questions.prompt: Which animation can use useNativeDriver: true?
choices: Animating opacity and a translateY transform
questions.explain: The native driver supports non-layout props such as opacity and transform. Layout props such as width and flex need a different approach.

questions.prompt: The input value is 150. What is the output?
questions.explain: With extrapolate set to clamp, values beyond the input range stay at the end of the output range.

questions.prompt: A JS-driven animation stutters while a list loads. Why?
choices: Each frame needs the JS thread, which is busy with the list work
questions.explain: Without the native driver, every frame is computed in JavaScript. Move it to the native driver or a UI-thread animation library.

questions.prompt: At 60 frames per second, how long is each frame?
questions.explain: 1000 ms / 60 ≈ 16.7 ms. Work longer than that on a busy thread drops frames.

questions.prompt: Row is wrapped in React.memo, but every row still re-renders when the parent does. Why?
choices: memo does not work in React Native
onPress is a new function each render, so props are never equal
questions.explain: memo compares props shallowly. A new arrow function each render changes the prop. Wrap the handler in useCallback.

questions.prompt: Why remove heavy console.log calls from release builds?
choices: They crash the app in release
They still cost time on the JS thread, especially when logging large objects
questions.explain: Logging serialises values and does work on the JS thread. Strip logs in release builds.

questions.prompt: Which AppState value means the user switched to another app?
questions.explain: AppState is active in the foreground and background when another app is in front. iOS also reports inactive briefly during transitions.

questions.prompt: The user has permanently denied camera access. What should the app do when they tap "Scan"?
choices: Explain why the camera is needed and offer a button that opens the app settings
Ask for the permission again in a loop
questions.explain: Once a permission is blocked, the system will not show the prompt again. Only the user can change it in settings.

questions.prompt: Can you rely on setInterval to sync data every minute while the app is in the background?
choices: Yes, if the interval is under a minute
No, the OS can suspend JavaScript in the background; use the platform background task APIs
questions.explain: The OS suspends backgrounded apps to save battery. Background work must go through the scheduled background task APIs, and even then timing is not guaranteed.

questions.prompt: Which query best matches how a user finds a submit button?
choices: Find the third Pressable in the tree
questions.explain: Querying by role and accessible name tests what users and screen readers see, and also checks accessibility.

questions.prompt: A unit test fails with "native module is null". What is the usual fix?
choices: Run unit tests on a phone
Mock the native module in the Jest setup
Delete the module from the app
questions.explain: Jest runs in Node without native code. Mock native modules so the JavaScript logic can be tested.

questions.prompt: What do end-to-end tests add over component tests?
choices: They drive the real built app on a simulator or device, including native code and navigation
questions.explain: End-to-end tests catch integration problems that unit tests cannot, at the cost of speed and flakiness.

questions.prompt: Which change can ship as an over-the-air update?
choices: Adding a new permission to the app config
Adding a new native camera library
Fixing a typo in a JavaScript screen
questions.explain: OTA updates replace the JavaScript bundle and assets only. Native changes need a new store build.

questions.prompt: Why must an OTA update target a matching runtime version?
choices: JavaScript that expects native code the installed binary lacks will crash
questions.explain: An update must only reach binaries with the native code it was built against. A runtime version makes that match explicit.

questions.prompt: A store rejects your upload even though the version is 2.1.0, a new version. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The build number was not increased
The app icon is too large
questions.explain: Every upload needs a new, higher build number, even if the user-facing version changes.

questions.prompt: An icon-only button shows a trash can. What should a screen reader hear?
choices: A label such as "Delete message" with the role button
questions.explain: Give icon-only controls an accessibilityLabel that says what they do, and an accessibilityRole of button.

questions.prompt: A close icon is 20 by 20 points and hard to tap. What is the simplest fix?
choices: Add hitSlop or padding so the touch target is about 44–48 points
questions.explain: Platform guidelines recommend touch targets of about 44 points or 48 dp. hitSlop grows the target without changing the layout.

questions.prompt: How do you tell a screen reader that a button is disabled?
choices: Set accessibilityState={{ disabled: true }} (or the disabled prop)
questions.explain: Colour alone is not announced. Expose the state so assistive tech reads "dimmed" or "disabled".

questions.prompt: You add a library with custom native code. Why can't you keep testing in the prebuilt Expo Go app?
choices: Expo Go does not run JavaScript
Expo Go only includes the native modules it was built with; you need a development build
Expo Go only works on Android
questions.explain: A development build is your own app binary with your native modules, plus the developer tools.

questions.prompt: What does prebuild (continuous native generation) do?
choices: Generates the native iOS and Android projects from your app config and plugins
Uploads the app to the stores
questions.explain: Native folders become generated output, so upgrades and config changes are repeatable instead of hand-edited.

questions.prompt: What is the main trade-off of a bare project?
choices: Full control of the native projects, but you maintain them yourself, including upgrades
questions.explain: Bare projects suit heavy native customisation. The cost is owning native build files and upgrade work.
